query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A brief, near-eutectic-temperature annealing step followed by rapid quenching will partially disrupt the continuous lamellar colony architecture by inducing moderate spheroidization at interphase boundaries and the formation of hierarchical subgrain structures. This microstructural modification will reduce local stress concentrations that initiate microcracking, thereby improving both room‐temperature tensile ductility and strength compared to the untreated state.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase, continuous lamellar colonies featuring numerous internal boundaries that serve as microcrack initiation sites under room-temperature tensile loads.
generation.intervention: Apply a brief annealing treatment near the eutectic temperature followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Anneal the alloy at a temperature proximate to its eutectic point for a short duration (on the order of minutes) in a controlled atmosphere, then quench rapidly to room temperature to freeze in the modified microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Partial disruption of lamellar continuity, moderate spheroidization at interphase boundaries, and the emergence of hierarchical subgrain structures.
generation.mechanism: The near-eutectic annealing allows sufficient atomic mobility to relax and slightly rearrange the interlamellar boundaries, reducing their continuity and smoothing sharp geometric features. Rapid quenching then preserves these beneficial microstructural changes, resulting in fewer stress concentrators and crack initiation sites under tensile deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated samples will exhibit both enhanced tensile ductility (due to reduced microcracking at modified boundaries) and maintained or improved yield and ultimate tensile strengths when compared to the untreated, continuously lamellar baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloys with continuous, dual-phase lamellar colonies and numerous internal boundaries that facilitate premature microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile testing.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only if the annealing temperature and time are carefully controlled to achieve partial, not complete, disruption of lamellar continuity. Deviations from near-eutectic conditions or insufficient quench rates may not produce the desired microstructural refinement, limiting efficacy.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and may depend on specific alloy compositions and processing parameters. There is also potential interplay with residual stresses and other microstructural features that has not been fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets of the eutectic high-entropy alloy with similar as-cast, dual-phase lamellar microstructures. Subject one set to the proposed near-eutectic annealing (e.g., anneal for several minutes at a temperature just below the eutectic point) followed by rapid quenching, while keeping the other set as the untreated control. Characterize the microstructures with SEM/TEM to verify the emergence of partial spheroidization and hierarchical subgrain structures, then perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Tensile properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation to failure
Microstructural analysis: degree of spheroidization at interphase boundaries, lamellar continuity, and subgrain structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in tensile ductility (e.g., a clear increase in elongation to failure) while maintaining or enhancing strength relative to the control, and if the expected modifications in the lamellar boundary structure (partial spheroidization and hierarchical subgrain formation) are not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) established AlCoCrFeNi2.1 as a promising eutectic HEA with dual-phase lamellar colonies, but still found limits in room-temperature ductility. Subsequent research (PMC5818523, PMC6353877) introduced cryo-rolling, warm-rolling, and annealing to refine and hierarchically organize the L12+B2 lamellae, achieving strength–ductility improvements. More advanced processing (PMC6687781) combined cryogenic and warm deformation to create dual-heterogeneous microstructures with high strength and moderate ductility. Despite these advances, intermittent room-temperature microcracking initiation at lamella interfaces remains a key issue limiting widespread application.
decision.unsolved: Although multiple thermomechanical routes have enhanced strength and ductility, the fundamental challenge of microcracking at internal lamellar boundaries persists. The lamellar interfaces remain susceptible to crack initiation under tensile loading at room temperature, preventing full realization of reliable ductility and toughness in these eutectic high-entropy alloys.
decision.lever: Adopt a brief, near-eutectic-temperature annealing step followed by rapid quenching to partially disrupt lamellar continuity, induce moderate spheroidization at interphase boundaries, and promote hierarchical subgrain formation. Coupling this short-cycle homogenization with controlled cooling will refine internal boundary structures to reduce stress concentrations and enhance crack blunting while retaining lamellar-induced strength.
decision.why: Prior studies indicate that refining lamellae, reducing interfacial continuity, and introducing hierarchical features can mitigate brittle crack initiation without sacrificing the inherent strength benefits of the dual-phase microstructure. This short-cycle treatment exploits insights from recent thermomechanical design strategies (PMC5818523, PMC6687781) and addresses the unresolved problem of microcracking by lowering local stress concentrations at boundaries. The hypothesis is that partial spheroidization and carefully tuned boundary characteristics will maintain or improve strength while substantially boosting the alloy’s ductility at room temperature. A falsifying experiment is to measure tensile properties and fracture surfaces following the proposed treatment: if cracks still initiate early at lamellar boundaries and ductility remains unchanged compared to the unmodified baseline, then the hypothesis is disproven.
